impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that licenses exclusive commercialization rights but retains the right to sue third parties for infringement possesses sufficient constitutional standing to bring an infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who retains exclusionary rights—including the right to independently sue for infringement—satisfies the irreducible constitutional minimum of Article III standing, even after granting an exclusive license for manufacture, use, and sale. This clarifies standing requirements for patent holders who structure licenses to share enforcement authority with licensees.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners can structure license agreements to retain meaningful enforcement rights, ensuring they maintain standing to sue infringers independently even after granting broad exclusive licenses.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers face the prospect of suits from both licensees and patent owners when license agreements split enforcement rights, potentially increasing litigation exposure.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's anti-CGRP antibody headache patents were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112, after a jury found willful infringement and no invalidity.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity of Teva's headache treatment patents, reinstating the jury's findings of willful infringement and validity. The case involves blockbuster migraine drugs (Teva's Ajovy vs. Lilly's competing product) and has major implications for the pharmaceutical industry's ability to patent genus claims for antibody therapies based on functional characteristics.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies benefit from a more favorable standard for written description and enablement of antibody genus claims, protecting broad patent coverage for biologic therapies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar developers face stronger patent barriers when seeking to enter markets for antibody-based therapeutics, as broad genus claims are more likely to withstand validity challenges.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was legally sufficient evidence to support the jury's finding that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether the patent invalidity finding should be reversed where the alleged inventive contribution consisted of generally known information.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims, holding that the plaintiff failed to show its asserted trade secrets were protectable because the information was generally known in the field. The court also reversed the patent invalidity finding, reasoning that ideas found to be generally known cannot constitute an inventive contribution for inventorship purposes. The permanent injunction and exemplary damages were vacated.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from a reinforced requirement that plaintiffs must demonstrate their asserted trade secrets are not generally known, providing a meaningful defense threshold.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection must ensure rigorous documentation that their information is genuinely secret and not merely a compilation of generally known elements, or risk losing both trade secret and related patent claims.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. Ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a jury verdict form that combined infringement questions for multiple patents into a single question, without requiring the jury to identify which patent was infringed, requires vacatur of the infringement and damages judgments.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated an $11.5 million patent infringement judgment and remanded for a new trial, holding that a verdict form combining infringement questions for all asserted patents into a single question was reversible error. The court also remanded for further proceedings on § 101 eligibility under Alice step two for one patent while affirming eligibility for two others. The decision reinforces the importance of patent-specific jury findings in multi-patent cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement that jury verdicts must separately identify which patents are infringed, preventing ambiguous general verdicts that could sweep in invalid or non-infringed patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders pursuing multi-patent infringement cases face increased procedural complexity and the risk that aggregated verdict forms will lead to vacatur, even after securing favorable jury verdicts.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using relay devices on farming equipment are directed to patent-ineligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in finding the case was not exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data collection patents were invalid as directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under § 101 but vacated the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional, remanding for reconsideration of attorney fees under § 285. The decision continues the trend of invalidating patents that claim data collection and processing on conventional hardware, particularly in agricultural technology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of infringing data-collection patents benefit from continued robust application of § 101, and the remand on exceptionality signals that defending against clearly ineligible patents may warrant fee-shifting.
impacts.negativeImplications: Agtech and IoT companies seeking to patent data collection and processing systems face heightened § 101 risk, and the remand on fees increases the stakes of asserting patents that may be found ineligible.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL of non-infringement and no damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of eligibility for certain patent claims relating to non-uniform signal constellations used in digital communications while affirming eligibility for others, affirmed infringement findings, and affirmed the damages award. The case involves foundational wireless communication technology used in television broadcasting standards, with significant implications for standards-essential patent licensing.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims tied to specific technical implementations of communication standards received affirmation of infringement and damages, supporting enforcement of technology patents in standards-based industries.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies implementing communication standards face continued patent infringement exposure, and the split eligibility ruling creates uncertainty about which types of signal-processing claims survive § 101 challenges.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and in striking damages expert theories for inadequate disclosure in damages contentions.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the district court's summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's multi-core processor patent asserted against Intel, finding genuine issues of material fact on the extraterritoriality question, while affirming other aspects. The decision addresses the territorial reach of U.S. patent law for semiconductor products designed domestically but manufactured abroad, a critical issue for the global semiconductor industry.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting infringement of processor and semiconductor patents benefit from a broader view of domestic acts sufficient to establish infringement, even when manufacturing occurs overseas.
impacts.negativeImplications: Semiconductor companies with global manufacturing operations face increased infringement risk in the U.S. for products with domestic design components, even if physical production occurs abroad.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages models and in overturning a jury's breach of contract damages award in a case involving misappropriation of automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously excluded damages models. The court reversed the district court's post-trial reduction of breach of contract damages and reinstated the original jury award. The court affirmed Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation. The case involves significant software IP developed for vehicle manufacturing configuration.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software developers and licensors benefit from the reinstatement of jury damages awards and broader acceptance of damages methodologies in trade secret cases, strengthening enforcement of IP rights in technology licensing relationships.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop in-house replacements for licensed software face heightened trade secret misappropriation risk and potential exposure to larger damages awards under both unjust enrichment and reasonable royalty theories.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before Insulet brought suit alleging misappropriation of insulin pump trade secrets by former employees hired by a competitor.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court and held that Insulet's DTSA claim was time-barred, granting JMOL to EOFlow. The court found that Insulet knew or should have known of the alleged misappropriation more than three years before filing suit, based on publicly available information about its former employees' activities at EOFlow. This is a significant ruling on DTSA statute of limitations, particularly regarding when the discovery clock begins running.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation through hiring competitors' employees gain a stronger statute of limitations defense when the plaintiff had constructive knowledge of the alleged misappropriation from publicly available information.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders must act promptly upon learning of potential misappropriation, as publicly available indicators of competitor activity using former employees may trigger the limitations period even before direct evidence of actual misappropriation is obtained.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify to matters outside personal knowledge for purposes of summary judgment, and whether computer source code constitutes hearsay under the Federal Rules of Evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that a 30(b)(6) corporate deposition witness may testify beyond personal knowledge at summary judgment and that computer source code (as opposed to descriptive comments within it) is not hearsay. The ruling has broad implications for patent invalidity defenses based on prior commercial activity.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent cases benefit from expanded evidentiary options at summary judgment, including the ability to rely on 30(b)(6) testimony from corporate representatives who joined the company after relevant events, and the admissibility of source code as non-hearsay evidence.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face an increased risk of invalidity at summary judgment, as defendants can more easily prove prior commercial sales through corporate representative testimony and source code evidence, even when original witnesses are unavailable.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action when it previously missed the deadline for seeking a stay of the original action involving the same parties and issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for a mandatory stay under § 1659(a) by voluntarily dismissing a district court declaratory judgment action and refiling a new one to restart the clock. The decision prevents strategic manipulation of the stay provision and preserves parallel litigation tracks between ITC and district court proceedings in pharmaceutical patent disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders bringing ITC complaints benefit from certainty that respondents cannot game the mandatory stay provision to delay parallel district court proceedings, preserving access to faster judicial resolution of safe harbor and non-infringement defenses.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents lose a potential tactical option and must be diligent about exercising stay rights within the statutory window, or forfeit the ability to obtain a mandatory stay of concurrent district court litigation.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether the patentee was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding of no infringement of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents, agreeing that the pH claim limitation must be measured at the standard temperature recognized in the field (25°C) and that Actelion was barred from asserting the doctrine of equivalents. The decision has important implications for pharmaceutical patent claim drafting, particularly regarding measurement conditions for chemical properties.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic drug companies benefit from a clear interpretation that chemical property claims are measured under field-standard conditions, providing predictability when designing around pharmaceutical patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical patent holders must draft claims with explicit measurement conditions or risk narrow interpretation tied to industry-standard temperatures, potentially leaving room for competitors to formulate products that differ only under non-standard measurement conditions.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a third party that was not served in the underlying patent infringement litigation could file IPR petitions challenging patents asserted against another entity, and whether the Board's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination invalidating FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent claims and remanded for further proceedings. The case involves Qualcomm filing IPR petitions challenging patents asserted against Roambee on Roambee's filing deadline, raising concerns about third-party IPR petitions filed as proxies. The court declined to review the Board's denial of FedEx's motion to terminate the IPR proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from the vacatur of an obviousness finding, and the case highlights potential procedural protections against third-party IPR petitions that may be filed as surrogates for the actual defendant in litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking to use IPR as a defensive tool through third-party petitioners face uncertainty about the continued viability of this strategy, and the remand creates additional costs and delay.

impacts.caseName: National Veterans Legal Services Program v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users, including the propriety of attorneys' fees and incentive awards to nonprofit class representatives.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's approval of a $125 million settlement in a nationwide class action alleging the federal judiciary improperly used PACER fees to fund unrelated court technology projects. The court upheld the settlement as fair and reasonable, approved attorneys' fees, and affirmed incentive awards to the three nonprofit class representatives. The decision resolves a long-running dispute affecting hundreds of thousands of PACER users.
impacts.positiveImplications: The settlement provides substantial reimbursement to businesses and law firms that are heavy PACER users, and the affirmance of the settlement structure provides a template for future government overcharge class actions.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents are invalid for omission of a coinventor when the patent holder acknowledges the coinventor's contribution but cannot locate the coinventor to correct inventorship under 35 U.S.C. § 256.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that two patents were invalid due to the omission of a coinventor, where the patent holder acknowledged the contribution but was unable to locate the missing coinventor to correct inventorship under § 256. The court upheld the denial of a motion to judicially correct inventorship under § 256(b), holding that the patent holder had not demonstrated sufficient diligence in locating the missing inventor.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers gain a clear defense when patent holders cannot demonstrate diligence in locating and adding acknowledged coinventors, particularly in cases involving foreign contributors.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that collaborate with foreign manufacturers or contractors on inventions must maintain current contact information for all contributors and promptly correct inventorship, or risk patent invalidation.
